summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs every step of a trans visitor's stay in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force since 1 November 2024, it lets adults over 18 change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, placement reform or ordinance is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full, including to short-term visitors and their documents at check-in and border or identity checks.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure in this state. An analysis published on Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 sets out the operative rule under the SBGG: placement follows the prisoner's legal gender entry unless state law provides otherwise, with Länder statutes differing on whether they carry an abstract exception clause or one drafted specifically for trans prisoners. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is the site of the flashpoint case under that framework, a July 2026 ruling of the Landgericht Neubrandenburg that ordered placement in a men's prison despite the prisoner's completed legal gender change.

The outcome has gone the other way elsewhere in Germany, and the resulting political pressure is live. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, was transferred to a men's prison after extradition from Czechia, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility and critics characterising the gender change as an abuse of the law. France24 reported the same day that Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded by launching a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, the statute that applies in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as in every other Land.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which, according to her account reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she gave the publication a copy of her statement to the airport. Frankfurt is a common entry point for visitors arriving in northern Germany.

The partner baseline is the federal one as well: same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available since 1 October 2017, implementing legislation having been passed on 30 June 2017.
tangentialFactors:
Several other Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, so the placement picture across Germany is uneven rather than uniform. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. A new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

Earlier reporting sets the tone for how courts and prosecutors treat trans prisoners. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women after the new law followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists nationally: the German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern live under the same federal statute as visitors, but the prison-placement question bears on them directly: the July 2026 Landgericht Neubrandenburg ruling ordered a male-prison assignment against a completed legal gender change, which is the concrete exposure a resident faces if prosecuted in this state.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection.

Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Trans people in custody in Berlin have an official information page from the Berlin prison service setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities. No equivalent Mecklenburg-Vorpommern prison-service information page for trans detainees is recorded in the sources.

Since 1 January 2019 a 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, and in April 2019 it was clarified as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern prison act carries an abstract exception clause or a trans-targeted one, and how the Neubrandenburg ruling is applied at intake in facilities elsewhere in this state, is unresolved in the sources; the Verfassungsblog analysis describes the Länder-level split but does not set out this Land's statutory wording.

The long-term effect of the Bundesrat initiative announced by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to tighten the Self-Determination Act is not sourced; no amended federal text or adoption date is recorded.

The Wikipedia entry dedicated to Mecklenburg-Vorpommern yields no trans-relevant finding, so state-level administrative practice, complaint mechanisms and local facility conditions rest on the federal and comparative material rather than on any Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific documentation.

No data is available on how often placement decisions in this state depart from a prisoner's legal gender entry, or on outcomes for visitors held overnight in police custody here.
